overview: This bill bans kickbacks connected to pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, the companies that run prescription drug benefits for employer health plans. Under the bill, a PBM working for an employer plan could not pay anyone, such as an insurance broker or consultant, for steering the plan's business to it, keeping or renewing that business, or influencing how the plan picks a PBM. Any payment from a PBM to a broker, consultant or advisor would be presumed to be improper unless the parties can show with records made at the time that it was fair pay for real services unrelated to winning the business. The change is made to ERISA, the federal law that governs employer benefit plans, and would apply to plan years starting after it becomes law. As of July 2, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was awaiting a vote by the full House.
for: Supporters say brokers and consultants who advise employers should not be paid by the PBMs they are supposed to be evaluating, and banning these payments helps employers and workers get unbiased advice and better drug benefit deals.
against: Critics say presuming every payment is improper could sweep in legitimate service fees and add paperwork, and that it targets only one part of drug pricing without lowering what patients pay at the pharmacy.
